syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

book.title: Ganita Manjari
book.edition: NCERT (reprint year not stated in the prelims)

chapters.title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

topics.title: The history of grid-based thinking and coordinates

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how early grid layouts and reference meridians worked as coordinate systems in practice.
Identify the contributions of Brahmagupta, Aryabhata, Descartes and others to the idea of coordinates.

topics.title: Coordinate axes, the origin and points on the axes

concepts.learning_objective: State the meaning of the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin, and the sign convention for distances from O.
Locate points of the form (x, 0) and (0, y) and find lengths along an axis on a scaled plan.

topics.title: Quadrants and the order of coordinates

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the quadrant of a point from the signs of its coordinates.
Explain why (x, y) and (y, x) are the same point only when x = y.
Find the distance between points on a line parallel to an axis and the distance of a point from an axis.
Use the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem to find the distance between any two points in the plane.
Find the image of a point reflected in an axis and explain why reflection preserves lengths.
Find the midpoint of a segment, or an unknown endpoint, from the coordinates of the points.
Check whether three points lie on one straight line using distances between them.
Identify the terms, variables, coefficients and constant term of an algebraic expression.
Find the degree of a one-variable polynomial and classify it as constant, linear, quadratic or cubic.

topics.title: Linear polynomials, linear equations and input-output processes

concepts.learning_objective: Evaluate a polynomial by substituting a value of the variable, viewing it as an input-output process.
Form and solve a linear equation by equating a linear polynomial to a constant in a word problem.
Recognise a linear pattern as a sequence whose consecutive terms have a constant difference.
Find and use a linear expression in n for the nth term of a growing pattern.
Model a quantity that increases by a fixed amount over equal intervals with a linear function.
Model a quantity that decreases by a fixed amount over equal intervals with a linear function.
Find a and b in y = ax + b from two pairs of values of x and y.
Interpret a as the rate of change and b as the fixed starting value in a real-life linear relationship.

topics.title: Visualising linear relationships: slope and y-intercept

concepts.learning_objective: Plot y = ax + b using two points and check whether a point lies on the line.
Identify the slope a and y-intercept b of y = ax + b and describe how they change the line.
Recognise that lines with equal slopes and different y-intercepts are parallel.

topics.title: The need to count: natural numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how one-to-one correspondence allowed early humans to count and record quantities.
Identify early evidence of number use such as the Ishango bone and the Vedic names for powers of 10.
Decide whether natural numbers are closed under a given operation, using counterexamples.
Describe how the idea of shunyata and the Bakhshali manuscript led to zero as a number.
Apply Brahmagupta's rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero.
Describe integers as fortunes (dhana), debts (rina) and zero, and the symbol Z.
Use Brahmagupta's rules of signs to add, subtract and multiply integers in real-life contexts.
State the definition of a rational number p/q and explain why q must not be zero.
Test whether two rational numbers are equal using the rule ad = bc.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rational numbers and use their closure properties.

topics.title: Rationals on the number line, absolute value and density

concepts.learning_objective: Locate rational numbers on the number line by dividing unit intervals into equal parts.
Find absolute values and the distance |a - b| between two rational numbers.
Find rational numbers between two given rationals using averages and explain density.
Follow the proof by contradiction that the square root of 2 is irrational.
Construct lengths such as the square roots of 2 and 3 on the number line using right triangles.
Describe pi as irrational and evaluate partial sums of Madhava's series.
Predict from the denominator's prime factors whether a rational number's decimal terminates or repeats.
Convert pure and general repeating decimals into the form p/q.
Distinguish rational and irrational numbers by their decimal expansions and describe the real numbers.
Distinguish an algebraic identity, true for all values of its variables, from an equation.
Interpret (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² using a square of side (a + b) partitioned into squares and rectangles.
Use (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² to expand binomials and evaluate squares of numbers.
Factorise perfect-square trinomials, taking out a common factor first where needed.
Use (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² to factorise expressions and compute squares.
Use identities to prove patterns among squares of consecutive numbers.

topics.title: More identities: (a + b + c)² and a² − b²

concepts.learning_objective: Expand and apply (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
Apply a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), and Shridharacharya's form a² = (a + b)(a − b) + b², to quick calculations.

topics.title: Factorisation with algebra tiles and by splitting the middle term

concepts.learning_objective: Represent products and factors of quadratic expressions with algebra tiles.
State and use (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.
Factorise quadratic expressions by splitting the middle term using a + b and ab.
Use (a + b)³ and (a − b)³ to expand and to recognise perfect cubes.
Apply x³ − y³ = (x − y)(x² + xy + y²) and x³ + y³ = (x + y)(x² − xy + y²).
Use x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − xz − yz) to evaluate expressions.
Simplify rational algebraic expressions by factorising and cancelling non-zero common factors.
Form and factorise quadratic expressions to solve area problems.

chapters.title: I’m Up and Down, and Round and Round

topics.title: Definitions and symmetries of a circle

concepts.learning_objective: Define a circle as the locus of points on a plane equidistant from a given point, and identify its centre and radius.
Identify chords and diameters and recognise the diameter as the longest chord.
Describe the complete rotational symmetry of a circle and its lines of reflection symmetry.

topics.title: Circles through given points and the circumcircle

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why infinitely many circles pass through two points, with centres on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
Explain why exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points and locate the circumcentre of a triangle.

topics.title: Chords and the angles they subtend at the centre

concepts.learning_objective: Use congruence to show that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, and conversely.

topics.title: Midpoints and perpendicular bisectors of chords

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the results that the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.

topics.title: Distance of chords from the centre

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the results that equal chords are equidistant from the centre and equidistant chords are equal.
Compare distances of unequal chords from the centre and compute chord lengths using the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.
Distinguish major and minor arcs by the angle they subtend at the centre.
Apply the theorem that the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle at any point on the circle outside the arc.
Use the corollary that a diameter subtends a right angle at any point on the circle.
Determine when four points are concyclic using equal angles subtended by a segment.
Apply the result that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, and its converse.

topics.title: Perimeter of shapes and the C/D ratio

concepts.learning_objective: Find the perimeter of squares, rectangles and equilateral triangles and see that perimeter-to-side ratios are fixed.
Explain that the ratio of circumference to diameter is the same for all circles and estimate it by measurement.
Describe how approximations of pi developed from ancient civilisations to Madhava's exact series.
Recognise that pi, like root 2, cannot be written as a ratio of two integers.
Distinguish between a close rational approximation of pi and its exact value.
Use C = 2πr to find circumferences, including on an athletics track.
Find the length of an arc subtending θ° at the centre using 2πr × θ/360.
Solve perimeter problems built from circular arcs and semicircles.

topics.title: Area of rectangle, parallelogram and triangle

concepts.learning_objective: Find the area of a parallelogram as base × height.
Find and apply the area of a triangle as half base × height.
Use the theorem that a median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
Find the area of a triangle from its three sides using Heron's formula.
Relate the area of a triangle to the radii of its incircle and circumcircle.

topics.title: Brahmagupta's formula and squaring a rectangle

concepts.learning_objective: Find the area of a cyclic 4-gon from its sides using Brahmagupta's formula.
Explain how Heron's formula is a special case of Brahmagupta's formula.
Explain Baudhayana's construction of a square equal in area to a rectangle.

topics.title: Area of a circle and of a sector

concepts.learning_objective: Find the area of a circle using A = πr² and explain why the formula holds.
Find the area of a sector as πr² × θ/360.
Explain that the ratio of perimeter squared to area depends only on shape, not size.

chapters.title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

concepts.learning_objective: Identify a random experiment as one whose possible outcomes are known but whose result in a single trial cannot be predicted.
Explain probability as a measure of how likely an event is, distinguishing subjective judgement from objective estimates.
State that probability lies on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Describe and rank events as impossible, less likely, even chance, more likely or certain.
Calculate experimental probability as the number of times an event occurred divided by the total number of trials.
Distinguish the frequency of an event from its relative frequency in observed data.
Decide whether the outcomes of an experiment are equally likely.
Calculate theoretical probability as favourable outcomes divided by possible outcomes.

topics.title: Statistical data, sampling and the long run

concepts.learning_objective: Estimate probabilities from sample data and use them to make predictions for a population.
Explain that experimental probability tends towards theoretical probability as the number of trials increases.
Recognise that independent trials have no memory, so past results do not change the next probability.
Write the sample space of an experiment, listing every outcome exactly once, and find its size n(S).
Identify an event as a subset of the sample space and list its outcomes.
Use a tree diagram to list all outcomes of a multi-step experiment.
Find probabilities of events in multi-step experiments using a tree diagram.

chapters.title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

topics.title: Introduction to sequences and their notation

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the terms of a sequence using position notation such as t1, t2, ..., tn and distinguish finite from infinite sequences.
Describe the patterns in triangular and square numbers as sums of natural numbers and odd numbers.
Use an explicit formula in n to compute any term of a sequence directly.
Decide whether a number is a term of a sequence by solving tn = k for a natural number n.
Generate terms of a sequence from a recursive rule that relates each term to earlier terms.
Recognise the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence, its rule Vn = Vn-1 + Vn-2 and its history.
Identify an arithmetic progression and its common difference, including negative differences.
Apply tn = a + (n - 1)d to find terms, positions and unknown first terms or differences of an AP.
Explain why the points (n, tn) of an AP lie on a straight line.

topics.title: Sum of the first n natural numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Derive and use Sn = n(n + 1)/2 by pairing the sum with its reverse.
Find the sum of a block of consecutive natural numbers as a difference of two such sums.
Identify a geometric progression by checking that the ratio of consecutive terms is constant.
Apply tn = ar^(n-1) to find terms and positions of terms in a GP.
Model repeated multiplication, such as the heights of a bouncing ball, with a GP.

topics.title: Fun with fractals: the Sierpinski triangle and carpet

concepts.learning_objective: Find the number of shaded pieces at each stage of a Sierpinski fractal as a GP.
Find the shaded area at each stage of a Sierpinski fractal and describe how it shrinks towards 0.
